name: Valentinus
knownFor: A teacher at Rome from around 140 who broke with the church, placed the Maker of this world below a higher, unseen God, and founded the Valentinian school, against which Irenaeus of Lyon wrote his five books Against Heresies.
dates: At Rome from about the time of Bishop Hyginus to Bishop Anicetus
role: Teacher and founder of a school

keyWorks.title: Letters
keyWorks.about: known only from passages Clement of Alexandria quotes in his Stromata, among them the letter that compares the heart to an inn fouled by its guests

keyWorks.title: Homily
keyWorks.about: a passage Clement quotes in Stromata, Book 4, telling his hearers they are immortal by nature and that death will die in them

keyWorks.title: Psalm
keyWorks.about: quoted in the Refutation of All Heresies, Book 6, on all things hanging from spirit: the flesh from the soul, the soul from the air, the air from the upper air

traces: Irenaeus of Lyon calls the school of Ptolemy a bud from that of Valentinus and names Heracleon beside Ptolemy. Clement of Alexandria calls Heracleon the most distinguished of the Valentinian school.

Tertullian of Carthage names Ptolemy, Heracleon (printed "Heraclean" in the English translation), Secundus and Marcus the magician as teachers who struck off on paths of their own, and Axionicus at Antioch as the one man in his day who still kept Valentinus's rules in full.
Tertullian calls the Valentinians a very large body of heretics.
remembered: Irenaeus says he adapted the principles of the Gnostic teaching to his own school, and held that whoever overthrew the Valentinians overthrew every kind of heresy.
Tertullian names the writers who had already answered the school: Justin, Miltiades, Irenaeus and Proculus.
Tertullian calls him a disciple of Platonism, beside Marcion the student of Stoicism.
The Refutation of All Heresies says Valentinus claimed to have seen a newborn child who told him he was the Word.

uncertain: Almost everything known of him comes from his opponents: Irenaeus of Lyon, Tertullian of Carthage, Clement of Alexandria and the Refutation of All Heresies. His own words survive only in the few passages they quote, most of them in Clement, who quotes them in order to answer them.

On two points of his teaching Irenaeus and Clement agree: the Maker of this world set below a higher, unseen God, and a class of people saved by nature. Clement stands on Valentinus's own letters and homily. He had also read Irenaeus, Eusebius of Caesarea says, so the two are not wholly independent.

The heaven of divine powers in pairs, and the fall of one of them, rest on Irenaeus; Clement does not confirm them. The Refutation of All Heresies also sets out a system, but it copies long passages of Irenaeus in its Book 6, as a note in the American edition says, so it is not a second witness. Tertullian, in Against the Valentinians, says he follows Irenaeus among the earlier writers.
The story of the lost bishopric is Tertullian's alone, and he tells it to show a man driven by ambition and revenge.
Around 140 is approximate. Irenaeus has him arrive in the time of Hyginus, and Eusebius of Caesarea puts the start of Hyginus's time as bishop in the first year of Antoninus Pius.
Tertullian places him at Rome under Bishop Eleutherus. Irenaeus places him from Hyginus to Anicetus, earlier.
Irenaeus says that Cerdo arrived at Rome in the time of Hyginus. Of Marcion he says only that he succeeded Cerdo and flourished under Anicetus.
That he was taught by Theudas, a pupil of Paul, is his followers' claim, as Clement reports it.
No source we hold says where he was born.

briefReferences: Irenaeus of Lyon, Against Heresies III.4.3, tr. Alexander Roberts and W. H. Rambaut: Valentinus came to Rome in the time of Hyginus and remained until Anicetus; Cerdo arrived in the time of Hyginus, and Marcion succeeded him.
Eusebius of Caesarea, Church History IV.10, tr. Arthur Cushman McGiffert: Hyginus bishop of Rome from the first year of Antoninus Pius, for around 140.

Tertullian of Carthage, Against the Valentinians 4, tr. Peter Holmes: the name Valentinians; he expected to be made bishop as an able and eloquent man; a confessor chosen instead; the break; ambition and revenge.
Irenaeus, Against Heresies I.11.1: he adapted the Gnostic teaching to his own school; the pairs of powers; one falling and producing the rest of the universe; the Demiurge below.
Clement of Alexandria, Stromata II.3, tr. William Wilson, and Irenaeus, Against Heresies I.6.2: his followers give faith to the simple and claim knowledge for themselves, saved by nature.

Clement, Stromata II.8, II.20, IV.13 and VI.6, tr. Wilson: Valentinus's own letters, homily and book quoted and answered; the heart like a caravanserai, fouled by its guests and the abode of many demons; "But when the only good Father visits it, it is sanctified, and gleams with light."
Refutation of All Heresies VI, tr. J. H. MacMahon: a psalm of Valentinus quoted word for word, and his vision of a newborn child.
Eusebius, Church History VI.13, tr. McGiffert: Clement gives extracts from Irenaeus.
Clement, Stromata IV.13, tr. Wilson: a class saved by nature; the world below the living Aeon; the Creator as "Painter", to the glory of the invisible One.
Irenaeus, Against Heresies I preface 2 and II.4.1, and Clement, Stromata IV.9: Ptolemy's school a bud from Valentinus's; Ptolemy and Heracleon.

Irenaeus, Against Heresies I preface 2: he read the disciples' Commentaries and met some of them; feared believers would be carried off, since their language resembles the church's while their meaning differs.
Irenaeus, Against Heresies I to V, and IV preface 2-3: the five books; earlier writers failed for want of knowing the system; whoever overthrows the Valentinians overthrows every heresy.
World census, Valentinian & other Gnostic Christianities: his tradition.
